inline.s: The Buddha Lokeśvararāja, knowing that Dharmākara's wisdom was lofty, bright, and penetrating, and that his vows were deep, far-reaching, and vast, then proclaimed for him the merit, adornment, purity, and vast, perfect fulfillment of two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, the most exemplary of all. And according to his wish he displayed them to him one by one. In setting forth this Dharma, a thousand million years passed.
[That is, he proclaimed for him the lands of two hundred and ten million Buddhas] The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra (Wei translation) says:

“Then the Buddha Lokeśvararāja at once widely proclaimed the lands of two hundred and ten million Buddhas — the good and evil of their gods and humans, the coarse and the sublime of their lands — and in accord with his wish revealed them all to him.

[Thereupon Dharmākara, having heard what the Buddha said and seen it all, gave rise to supreme and peerless vows. Toward the good and evil of those gods and humans and the coarse and sublime of their lands, he pondered to the very end. Then, focusing his mind to oneness, he chose what he desired and brought his great vows to completion.]

At this time, as Dharmākara heard the Buddha Lokeśvararāja set forth each land one by one, and saw each Buddha-land thus revealed, he gave rise to the supreme and peerless vast vow to establish his own Buddha-land. Toward the good and evil of the gods and humans in those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, the coarse and the sublime of their lands, and all the rest, he pondered and investigated thoroughly. Focusing his mind to oneness, he chose what he himself desired and thereby formed the guiding plan for the land he would establish (brought his great vows to completion).

[With vigor and diligence he sought and searched, reverently and carefully he maintained it, cultivating merit and virtue until he fulfilled five kalpas. Toward the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he was clear and penetrating, as though they were a single Buddha-land. The Buddha-land he gathered in surpassed them all.]

Then, brave and diligent, he sought and searched with toil, and without slackening cultivated merit and virtue for fully five kalpas, completing the blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish (embodied in the forty-eight vows). Toward the merit and adornment of those two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he was clear and penetrating, as though they were a single Buddha-land. And the Buddha-land he would establish surpassed them all.
[The blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish] The Huishu of the Immeasurable Life Sutra says:
“Now then,
(an opening particle)
a bodhisattva establishes a pure land as a skilled craftsman builds a great city: first he ponders and draws it out.
Five kalpas of pondering — thus he drew it out.”
(Translation: a bodhisattva establishes the Buddha-land he will attain when he becomes a Buddha as a master architect builds a great city: first he thoughtfully draws out the blueprint.
The five kalpas through which Bhikṣu Dharmākara sought and cultivated virtue are exactly the drawing out of the blueprint of his own Buddha-land.)

[Having gathered it in, he again went to where the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja was. He bowed his head at his feet, circled the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, saying to the World-Honored One: I have accomplished the pure conduct that gathers in a Buddha-land.]

After Bhikṣu Dharmākara had completed the blueprint of the Buddha-land he would establish, he came once more to the dwelling of the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja. He bowed his head at his feet, circled the Buddha three times, and stood with palms joined, saying to the Buddha: I have accomplished the pure conduct of drawing out the blueprint of a Buddha-land.
[Gathering in] The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Life Sutra (Wei translation) says:
“May the Buddha widely proclaim the Dharma to me, that I may practice it and gather in a Buddha-land, a pure and adorned land of immeasurable wonder.”

[I have accomplished the pure conduct that gathers in a Buddha-land] After the Buddha Lokeśvararāja proclaimed for Bhikṣu Dharmākara and displayed to him the merit, adornment, purity, and vast, perfect fulfillment of two hundred and ten million Buddha-lands, he spent five kalpas drawing out the blueprint of his own Buddha-land (embodied in the forty-eight vows). After he made that blueprint public (set forth the forty-eight great vows), he then piled up merit and accumulated virtue, passing through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, and perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
[He piled up merit and accumulated virtue, passing through immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, and perfectly accomplished the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss] The preceding text says:

“In ages past, immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas ago, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world, teaching and liberating immeasurable sentient beings, causing them all to attain the way, and then entered extinction. Next there was a Tathāgata named Light Far-Reaching, then one named Moonlight, ......, then one named Lokasaṃbhava; all such Buddhas have already passed. At that time there next was a Buddha named the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja.”
“When he set forth this Dharma, a thousand million years passed”
Bhikṣu Dharmākara
) cultivated merit and virtue until he fulfilled five kalpas.”
The later text says:
“Dharmākara became a Buddha, named Amitābha. Since his attainment of Buddhahood, ten kalpas have passed to now.”

Therefore the time from Bhikṣu Dharmākara's piling up of merit and virtue to his perfect accomplishment was: immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas, minus the time the fifty-three Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṃkara dwelt in the world, and further minus a thousand million years, five kalpas, and ten kalpas. Seen from the standpoint of modern mathematics, the result is still immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas. Ordinarily, the time for a bodhisattva to cultivate the way and become a Buddha is three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, yet the time for Bhikṣu Dharmākara to cultivate the way and become a Buddha was instead immeasurable, inconceivable, countless kalpas — how many, many, many times more than three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, beyond all reckoning! This shows how immense the difficulty of establishing the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss was — truly inconceivable,
and therefore especially peerless
. Thus Amitābha Buddha is
“the most honored among lights, the king of Buddhas”
, and the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is
“supreme over countless Buddha-lands”

. The most peerless thing about the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss that Amitābha Buddha established is this: other Dharma-gates require one to cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought) before one can end birth and death and escape saṃsāra; whereas the Pure Land Dharma-gate needs only ten continuous mindful recitations of Amitābha Buddha at the end of life to move Amitābha Buddha to appear before one and lead one away, so that one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby ends birth and death and escapes saṃsāra (for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth
). Compared, the ease and difficulty of the two are no less than the gulf between heaven and an abyss! Therefore it is said:
“In the Dharma-ending age, of hundreds of millions upon millions who cultivate, scarcely one attains the way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation does one cross over birth and death.”

Moreover, once reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one has none of the many sufferings but receives every joy, and at once attains the stage of non-retrogression, until one becomes a Buddha. Therefore the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:

“This question of yours now surpasses in merit a hundred thousand million times the offering of alms to the arhats and pratyekabuddhas of one world, and the giving, through kalpas on end, to the gods and humans and to the flying and crawling creatures. Why is that? Because the gods and humans and every living being of the future will all, through your question, gain deliverance from birth and death.”

[Three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas] The time for a bodhisattva to become a Buddha. Kalpas are of three kinds, great, middling, and small; the kalpa spoken of here means a great kalpa, hence “three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.” As for the number of years in one asaṃkhyeya kalpa, if one reckons ten thousand ten-thousands as one yi and ten thousand yi as one zhao, then one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equals ten million ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand ten-thousand zhao great kalpas.

[The Buddha said: Excellent! Now is precisely the time. You should set it forth in full, to gladden the assembly. And let the great multitude, having heard this Dharma, obtain great and excellent benefit, and be able to cultivate and gather in a Buddha-land, fulfilling their immeasurable great vows.]

The Buddha Lokeśvararāja said with great delight: Excellent! Now is precisely the time; you should set it forth in detail, to gladden the assembly. And let the great multitude, having heard this Dharma, obtain great and excellent benefit, and be able to cultivate how to design their own Buddha-lands, so as to fulfill their immeasurable great vows to become Buddhas and establish lands.

[Excellent] This shows that the conduct of Bhikṣu Dharmākara deeply pleased the sage's mind, accorded with the Buddha's own heart, and broadly responded to the capacities of the assembly; and so he sighed in approval and praised him, saying “Excellent” — these are words of the Buddha's deep delight.
[Dharmākara said: I pray the World-Honored One, in great compassion, to hear and consider.]
Dharmākara reverently said to the Buddha: I pray the World-Honored One, in great compassion, to hear and consider.
Should I attain Buddhahood, and in my land there be hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(1. Vow That the Land Have No Evil Destinies)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and there be hells, hungry ghosts, or animals in my land, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Not attain perfect enlightenment] Then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land, after the end of their lives, again fall into the three evil paths, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(2. Vow That They Not Again Enter Evil Destinies)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land, after the end of their lives, again fall into the three evil paths, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not all possess bodies of true golden hue, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(3. Vow of Bodies of True Golden Hue)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land do not all possess bodies of true golden hue, then may I not become a Buddha.
[All]
Every one of them.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land differ in bodily form and countenance, and there be fair and ugly among them, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(4. Vow That None Be Fair or Ugly)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land differ in bodily form and countenance, and there be distinctions of fair and uncomely, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Fair and ugly] Fair and uncomely. “Ugly” here means that a thing is not good; for example, an ugly field. [That there be fair and ugly] That there be distinctions of fair and uncomely.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of knowing past lives, so that they know the affairs of a hundred thousand million nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(5. Vow of the Power of Knowing Past Lives)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of knowing past lives, so that they know the affairs of a hundred thousand million million kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Nayuta] The name of a number, equivalent to what is now called a yi.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the divine eye, so that they see a hundred thousand million nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(6. Vow of the Divine Eye)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the divine eye, so that they see a hundred thousand million million Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the divine ear, so that they hear what a hundred thousand million nayutas of Buddhas proclaim and do not all receive and uphold it, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(7. Vow of the Divine Ear)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the divine ear, so that they hear what a hundred thousand million million Buddhas proclaim and do not all receive and uphold it, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of knowing others' minds, so that they know the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand million nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(8. Vow of Knowing Others' Minds)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of knowing others' minds, so that they know the thoughts of the beings in a hundred thousand million million Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they can pass beyond a hundred thousand million nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(9. Vow of Unobstructed Travel)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land do not gain the power of unimpeded travel, so that in the space of a single thought they can pass beyond a hundred thousand million million Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land give rise to thoughts and covet and reckon the body, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(10. Vow of Not Coveting the Body)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land give rise to thoughts and covet and reckon the body, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Coveting and reckoning the body] Falsely clinging to a self that has a body (falling into the view of the body), and thereby coveting, reckoning, loving, hating, and judging accord and opposition. In cultivation, ordinary beings mostly fall into the view of the body; the view of the body is foremost among the delusions of view, and unless the delusions of view are cut off one cannot enter the stream of the sages. [Delusions of view] The delusions of view are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in understanding, such as the five wrong views: the view of the body, extremism, wrong views, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and ascetic practices.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not dwell in the state of the definite assembly and necessarily reach extinction, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(11. Vow of Dwelling in Right Concentration)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land do not dwell in right concentration and necessarily reach extinction, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Concentration] Short for “right concentration.” [The three assemblies] The three assemblies are three classes of sentient beings: the definite assembly (shortened to “concentration”), the wrong assembly, and the indefinite assembly. The definite assembly means those beings who will certainly awaken; the wrong assembly means those who ultimately cannot awaken; the indefinite assembly means those between right and wrong, who may or may not awaken. [
Necessarily reach extinction
] This means that the beings in the Land of Ultimate Bliss will all become Buddhas and, after turning the great wheel of Dharma, manifest extinction (enter nirvāṇa).
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and my radiance be limited, so that it does not illumine a hundred thousand million nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(12. Vow of Immeasurable Radiance)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and my radiance be limited, so that it does not illumine a hundred thousand million million Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and my lifespan be limited, even to a hundred thousand million nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(13. Vow of Immeasurable Buddha-Life)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and my lifespan be limited, even to a hundred thousand million million kalpas, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the śrāvakas in my land be countless, so that if all the beings of a billion-world universe became pratyekabuddhas and together, for a hundred thousand kalpas, reckoned and computed, they could know their number, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(14. Vow of Countless Śrāvakas)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the śrāvakas in my land be countless, so that if all the beings of a billion-world universe became pratyekabuddhas and together, for a hundred thousand kalpas, reckoned and computed, they could know their number, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land have a lifespan without limit — except by their own vows, in which case their length is
at their own disposal; if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(15. Vow of Immeasurable Lifespans for Beings)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land have a limitless lifespan — except by their own vows, in which case long and short are at their own disposal. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[If it were not so] If it were not thus.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land even hear of any unwholesome name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(16. Vow of Not Hearing Evil Names)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land even hear of any unwholesome name, then may I not become a Buddha.
even hear of any unwholesome name
] In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, unwholesome names do not so much as exist — how much less unwholesome things! Such is the peerless excellence of the Land of Ultimate Bliss!
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions do not all praise and extol my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(17. Vow That All Buddhas Praise Him)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions do not all praise and extol my name, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wish to be born in my land and even recite ten times, are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. Only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma are excepted.
(18. Vow That Ten Recitations Bring Certain Rebirth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the ten directions, with utmost sincerity and joyful faith, wish to be born in my land and even recite ten times, are not born there, then may I not become a Buddha. Only those who commit the five grave offenses and slander the right Dharma are excepted.

[Utmost sincerity] A heart utterly sincere and utterly firm. [Even ten recitations] This is an abbreviated way of saying “even at the end of life, ten continuous recitations calling my name.” As for the precise meaning of “even ten recitations” in the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo in his Collection of the Land of Peace and Bliss teaches:
“If there be a being who, though he has done evil all his life,
at the hour of death, with ten continuous recitations, calls my name
and is not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.”
, (For details see
Ten Recitations
The Eighteenth Vow
) [Ten continuous recitations] Reciting the name of Amitābha ten times with mind following mind, unmixed with deluded thoughts. Master Tanluan teaches:
“Unmixed with other thoughts
(unmixed with deluded thoughts)
, mind following upon mind
(mind succeeding mind
“even to ten recitations — this is called ten continuous recitations.”
He also says:
“With ten continuous recitations at the end of life, one at once attains rebirth.”
, (For details see
Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teaching

) [The five grave offenses] Five kinds of transgression utterly contrary to principle: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, shedding the Buddha's blood, and breaking the harmonious Saṅgha. Because these five are acts of extreme evil, and committing any one of them brings falling into the uninterrupted hell, they are also called “uninterrupted karma.”

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the ten directions who give rise to the bodhi-mind, cultivate every merit and virtue, and with utmost sincerity make vows wishing to be born in my land — if at the end of their lives I do not appear before them surrounded by a great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(19. Vow That Utmost Sincerity Brings Rebirth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the ten directions who give rise to the bodhi-mind, cultivate every merit and virtue, and with utmost sincerity make vows wishing to be born in my land — if at the end of their lives I do not appear before them surrounded by a great assembly, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, fix their thoughts on my land, plant the roots of every virtue, and with utmost sincerity dedicate the merit, wishing to be born in my land, do not thereby accomplish their wish, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(20. Vow That Fixed Thought Brings Certain Rebirth)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the beings of the ten directions who hear my name, fix their thoughts on my land, plant the roots of every virtue, and with utmost sincerity dedicate the merit, wishing to be born in my land,
do not accomplish their wish as they desire
then may I not become a Buddha.
[Roots of virtue] That is, roots of goodness. De means good, ben means root: the merit of every good and ten thousand practices is the root of the Buddha-fruit and bodhi. The Lotus Sutra says:
“At the places of the Buddhas, they plant the roots of every virtue.”
The Immeasurable Life Sutra says:
“Eliminating all outflows, they plant the roots of every virtue.”

[Dedication] “Turning one's own roots of goodness toward some goal” — gathering the roots of goodness one has created and directing them, with added power, toward a certain aim, so that it may swiftly be realized. For example, one dedicates all the good cultivated by one's three karmas (bodily, verbal, and mental) and even such various merits as repentance and entreaty to all beings of the Dharma-realm, that they may together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth says:
“To dedicate means to turn one's own merit and virtue and bestow it universally upon beings, that together they may see the Tathāgata Amitābha and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Shandao's Verses of Vowing to Take Refuge in the Three Treasures say:
“May this merit and virtue be bestowed equally upon all, that together we may give rise to the bodhi-mind and be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
(The Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles)
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land do not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great being, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(21. Vow of the Thirty-Two Marks)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land do not all possess the thirty-two marks of a great being, then may I not become a Buddha.

[The thirty-two marks of a great being] Also called the thirty-two marks of a great man: 1. level and even feet; 2. a thousand-spoked wheel on each foot; 3. long, slender fingers; 4. soft and supple hands and feet; 5. webbed hands and feet; 6. full and rounded heels; 7. high and well-formed insteps; 8. calves like those of a king of deer (
shuàn
the calf of the leg)

; 9. hands reaching past the knees; 10. the male organ concealed; 11. body broad and tall; 12. blue-black hair pores; 13. body hair curling upward; 14. a golden body; 15. a constant halo of one fathom; 16. fine, smooth skin; 17. the seven places full and rounded; 18. both armpits full; 19. a body like a lion's; 20. an upright and dignified body; 21. full and rounded shoulders; 22. forty teeth in the mouth; 23. white, even, and close-set teeth; 24. four pure white fangs; 25. a jaw (the palate bones that bear the teeth) like a lion's; 26. the finest flavors moistening the throat; 27. a broad, long tongue; 28. a pure and far-carrying Brahmā voice; 29. eyes of dark violet; 30. eyelashes like a bull king's; 31. a white curl between the brows; 32. a fleshy protuberance on the crown. [Violet (
gàn
) blue] A color that is red showing through black.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of one more rebirth — except by their own vows, for the sake of beings, donning the armor of the great vow and entering other worlds to freely liberate them all; roaming through the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, piling up roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, awakening and transforming sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
and establishing them in the supreme true path,
beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages
in succession, and manifesting the practice of Samantabhadra's virtues; if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(22. Vow of One More Rebirth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas of other Buddha-lands who come to be born in my land do not ultimately reach the stage of one more rebirth — except by their own vows, for the sake of beings, donning the armor of the great vow and going to other worlds to freely liberate all beings; roaming through the Buddha-lands, cultivating the bodhisattva conduct, piling up roots of virtue, and making offerings to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, and awakening and teaching sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, establishing them in the supreme true path, beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages in succession, and manifesting the practice of Samantabhadra's virtues; if it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[One more rebirth] To finish this one life and then take the Buddha's place — this is another name for the final-body bodhisattva (the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment). For example, the bodhisattva Maitreya now dwelling in the inner court of the Tuṣita heaven is a bodhisattva of one more rebirth. All beings reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss have immeasurable lifespans and in this one life attain Buddhahood; the “one life” spoken of refers to one life of fragmentary birth and death. But the “one life” in “to finish this one life and then take the Buddha's place” refers to one life of transformative birth and death. [Donning the armor of the great vow] They put on the great armor that adorns them with the merit of their vast vows. [Establishing them in the supreme true path] Teaching them to cultivate the Pure Land Dharma-gate. “The supreme true path”

refers to the Pure Land Dharma-gate, for the Pure Land Dharma-gate is perfect and direct, its skillful means ultimate, a single leap straight into the highest and most complete and sudden — and so it is called the supreme true path. Master Hanshan teaches:
“The one gate of the Pure Land embraces all three capacities; the sudden and the gradual alike enter it; no capacity is left out. This is what is meant by transcending the three realms horizontally;
it is the most supreme Dharma-gate
He also teaches:
“Of the Dharma-gates the Buddha taught for cultivating practice and escaping birth and death, there are many skillful means; only Buddha-recitation seeking birth in the Pure Land is
the most swift and essential
(Dream Roaming Collection,
Preface to the Guide to the Pure Land)

[Beyond the conduct of the ordinary stages in succession] Surpassing the practice of the common Dharma-gates that advance step by step in their ordinary order. In the cultivation of the common Dharma-gates, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages from ordinary being to Buddhahood, namely: the ten stages of faith, the ten stages of dwelling, the ten stages of practice, the ten stages of dedication, the ten stages of ground, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. But one who cultivates the Pure Land Dharma-gate and is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss sees the Buddha as the flower opens, awakens to the unborn, at once attains the patience with the unborn, and is established in the eighth ground. [The eighth ground] The eighth of the bodhisattva's ten grounds, called the Ground of Immovability. In this ground the bodhisattva dwells in the patience with the unborn, cuts off all exertion, and body and mind are quiescent and extinguished, like empty space; he accomplishes the pāramitā of vow and, with a nirvāṇa mind, is utterly still and unmoving — hence it is called the “Ground of Immovability.” [The ten grounds] The Ground of Joy, the Ground of Freedom from Defilement, the Ground of Radiance, the Ground of Blazing Wisdom, the Ground of Utmost Difficulty in Conquest, the Ground of Manifestation, the Ground of Far-Reaching, the Ground of Immovability, the Ground of Good Wisdom, and the Ground of the Dharma Cloud. These are the fifth set of ten among the bodhisattva's fifty-two stages of cultivation. In these ten grounds one gradually opens the realm of Buddhahood and accomplishes the wisdom of all modes; they already belong to the stage of the sages, and so they are also called the “ten sages.” [The three wisdoms] The wisdom of all, the wisdom of the paths, and the wisdom of all modes. The wisdom of all is the wisdom by which śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas understand the universal aspect of all dharmas, the universal aspect being the true nature of all dharmas; the wisdom of the paths is the wisdom by which bodhisattvas understand the various Dharma-gates of cultivation; the wisdom of all modes is the wisdom by which the Buddha penetrates both the universal and the particular aspects of all dharmas and transforms beings and cuts off delusion.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power to make offerings to all Buddhas, cannot in the space of one meal travel to immeasurable, countless millions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(23. Vow of Making Offerings to All Buddhas)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, relying on the Buddha's spiritual power to make offerings to all Buddhas, cannot in the space of one meal travel to immeasurable, countless millions of millions of Buddha-lands, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The space of one meal] The time of one meal. The Sutra of the Perfection of Wisdom,
Fascicle 347,

Chapter of Entrustment, divides time by length and brevity in turn into: one day and night, one day, half a day, one hour (equal to two hours today), a meal's duration, a moment, a while, and a snapping of the fingers.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, before all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue, and the offerings they require do not accord with their wishes, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(24. Vow That Offerings Follow the Mind)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, before all Buddhas, manifest their roots of virtue (roots of goodness), and the offerings they require do not accord with their wishes, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Offerings] Also called offerings and gifts: incense, flowers, food and drink, banners and canopies, and other such things offered to Buddhas and bodhisattvas. The Ratnakūṭa Sutra says:
“Bearing
(jī, to carry)
wondrous offerings, they present them to the Tathāgata and to the great assembly.”
The Lotus Sutra says:
“In ages to come, with all offerings, they shall make offerings and pay reverence.”
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land cannot expound the wisdom of all, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(25. Vow of Expounding Wondrous Wisdom)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land cannot expound the wisdom of all, then may I not become a Buddha.
[The wisdom of all] The wisdom that understands the universal aspect of all dharmas; the universal aspect is the true nature of all dharmas.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height, do not all gain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength, if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(26. Vow of Nārāyaṇa Bodies)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height, do not all gain bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength; if it were not so,
then may I not become a Buddha.
The bodhisattvas in my land, sixteen yojanas in height
] The Buddha Speaks of the Great Vehicle Immeasurable Life Adornment Sutra (Song translation) says:

“World-Honored One, when I attain bodhi and accomplish perfect enlightenment, and dwell in my jeweled land, all the bodhisattvas there shall be sixteen yojanas in height and gain the power of Nārāyaṇa. Their bodily marks shall be upright and adorned, their radiance shining, their roots of goodness complete, as they accomplish anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

[Bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength] Their bodies are as firm as adamant and their strength as inexhaustible as that of the god Nārāyaṇa; hence they are called bodies of adamantine Nārāyaṇa strength.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land, and all things there, be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, their forms and colors extraordinary, utterly subtle and wondrous beyond all reckoning, and the beings there, even having gained the divine eye, were any able to comprehend and distinguish their names and numbers, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(27. Vow That All Be Adorned and Pure)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land, and all things there, be adorned, pure, luminous, and beautiful, their forms and colors extraordinary, utterly subtle and wondrous beyond all reckoning; and the beings in the land, even having gained the divine eye, were any able to comprehend and distinguish their names and numbers, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Names and numbers]
The number of their names and kinds.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of but scanty merit and virtue, cannot know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi tree, four million li in height, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(28. Vow of Knowing and Seeing the Bodhi Tree)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land, even those of but scanty merit and virtue, cannot know and see the immeasurable light and color of the bodhi tree, four million li in height, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive and read the sutras, recite them, uphold them, and expound them do not gain eloquence and wisdom, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(29. Vow That Reciting the Sutras Brings Wisdom)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the bodhisattvas in my land who receive and read the sutras, recite them, uphold them, and expound them do not gain eloquence and wisdom, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land can be measured or limited, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(30. Vow of Unlimited Wisdom and Eloquence)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the wisdom and eloquence of the bodhisattvas in my land can be measured or limited, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and my land be pure, so that it reflects and reveals all the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as a bright mirror reveals the face — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(31. Vow of Reflecting the Ten Directions)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and my land be pure, so that it reflects and reveals all the immeasurable, countless, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as in a bright mirror one sees (beholds) the face. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and from the ground up to the empty air — palaces, towers, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and all the myriad things in my land — all be compounded together from immeasurable jewels and fragrances, adorned with wondrous beauty surpassing that of gods and humans, their fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the Buddha's conduct — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(32. Vow of Wondrous Adornment with Jewels and Fragrance)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and from the ground up to the empty air — palaces, towers, ponds, streams, flowers, and trees, and all the myriad things in my land — all be compounded together from immeasurable jewels and fragrances, adorned with wondrous beauty surpassing that of gods and humans, their fragrance pervading the worlds of the ten directions, and the bodhisattvas who smell it all cultivate the Buddha's conduct. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, touched in body by my radiance, are not made soft in body and mind, surpassing gods and humans — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(33. Vow That Those Touched by the Light Be Made Soft)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions, touched in body by my radiance, are not made soft in body and mind, surpassing gods and humans. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name do not gain the bodhisattva's patience with the unborn and all profound dhāraṇīs, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(34. Vow That Those Who Hear the Name Gain Patience)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the beings of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name do not gain the bodhisattva's patience with the unborn and all profound dhāraṇīs, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Patience with the unborn] Shortened to “patience with the unborn”: penetrating that all dharmas are fundamentally unborn, that sentient and insentient alike arise from conditions and have no nature of their own, and are in their very substance empty; and therefore dwelling at peace in the unborn Dharma without the mind stirring. [No nature of their own] Nature means substance; all dharmas have no substantial entity (and so are illusory), which is called having no nature of their own. The Lotus Sutra says:
“Knowing that all dharmas are ever without a nature of their own.”
The Śūraṅgama Sutra says:
“All illusions become without a nature of their own.”
[Dhāraṇī]
Upholding all dharmas, so that good dharmas are not lost and evil dharmas do not arise.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and in my land there be women; should women wish to be born in my land, they at once become men; and the countless gods and humans, and even the flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(35. Vow of No Women and Lotus Birth)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and in my land there be women; should women wish to be born in my land, they at once become men; and the countless gods and humans, and even the flying and crawling creatures, who come to be born in my land, are all born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels, and when grown are all bodhisattvas and arhats. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[That in my land there be women]
The Buddha Speaks of the Sutra of Amitābha, the Tathāgata of Threefold Enlightenment, the Sāl Tree, and Deliverance from the Human Path (Wu translation) says:

“The second vow: when I become a Buddha, let there be no women in my land. Should women wish to come to be born in my land, they at once become men. The countless gods, humans, and flying and crawling creatures who come to be born in my land shall all be born by transformation in lotus flowers in ponds of seven jewels. When grown they shall all be bodhisattvas and arhats, countless in number. If I gain this vow, then I shall become a Buddha; if I do not gain this vow, I shall never become a Buddha.”
The Buddha Speaks of the Immeasurable Pure and Equal Enlightenment Sutra (Han translation) says:

“In that land all are bodhisattvas and arhats; there are no women, and lifespans are exceedingly long, measureless countless kalpas. Women who are reborn there are born by transformation and all become men.”
[Countless] Without end.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, after the end of their lives, always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the Buddha-way — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(36. Vow of Always Cultivating Pure Conduct)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, after the end of their lives, always cultivate the pure conduct until they attain the Buddha-way. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Pure conduct]
Pure and undefiled action.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, throw themselves to the ground with the five limbs, bow their heads in reverence, rejoice in joyful faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, and the gods and people of the world do not all do them reverence — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(37. Vow That Gods and Humans Do Reverence)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the gods and humans of the immeasurable, inconceivable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions who hear my name, throw themselves to the ground with the five limbs, bow their heads in reverence, rejoice in joyful faith, and cultivate the bodhisattva conduct, and the gods and people of the world do not all do them reverence. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land wish to obtain clothing
(garments and adornment)

and it comes at once with the thought; as the Buddha praises, wondrous garments according with the Dharma are naturally on the body; and if there be any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(38. Vow That Wondrous Garments Follow the Thought)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the human beings and devas in my land wish to obtain clothing, and it comes at once with the thought, as the Buddha praises, wondrous garments according with the Dharma naturally on the body; and if there be any cutting, sewing, dyeing, or washing, then may I not become a Buddha.
[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the human beings and devas in my land receive a happiness not equal to that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(39. Vow of Joy Like That of the Outflow-Exhausted)
Should I attain Buddhahood
and the human beings and devas in my land receive a happiness not equal to that of a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, then may I not become a Buddha.

[Outflows exhausted] Having cut off every affliction (the delusions of view and thought). Outflow is another name for affliction. [The delusions of view and thought] The delusions of view and the delusions of thought. The delusions of view are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in understanding, such as the five wrong views: the view of the body, extremism, wrong views, grasping at views, and grasping at precepts and ascetic practices; the delusions of thought are ordinary beings' errors of confusion in thinking, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of sentient beings' birth and death through saṃsāra; cut them off and one can end birth and death and escape saṃsāra.

[Should I attain Buddhahood, and the bodhisattvas in my land who, as they wish, desire to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, do not at once have their wish fulfilled, seeing them all reflected in jewel trees as in a bright mirror one sees the face — if it were not so, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
(40. Vow of Lands Appearing in Trees)
Should I attain Buddhahood

and the bodhisattvas in my land who, as they wish, desire to see the immeasurable, adorned, and pure Buddha-lands of the ten directions, at once have their wish fulfilled, seeing them all reflected in jewel trees as in a bright mirror one sees the face. If it were not so, then may I not become a Buddha.
